header: PROPOSAL — NOT A CURRICULUM. An editor is expected to revise this file.
This is a first ordering of an A1-to-A2 isiXhosa course, written by an agent
from what the lexicon and the corpora can actually support. Nothing in it has
been approved by an isiXhosa editor, no isiXhosa appears in it at all, and no
row it produces is ever published: `molo content curate` writes units, skills,
lessons, exercises and sentences as `draft` and they wait for the dashboard.
Units are named for what a learner can then DO, not for a vocabulary field:
'Order food and drink', never 'Food vocabulary'. That is the CEFR can-do
framing and it is what the path banner shows. The vocabulary field lives in
`theme`, which is a key into `themes.json` and is read only by the curation
matcher.
The order is deliberate. The expected audience is visitors on a two- or
three-week trip and Norwegians with a family or work tie to South Africa, so
the situations a visitor meets in the first days come first: greeting, people,
things, food, getting around. Grammar rides along with the situation that
needs it rather than getting units of its own.
What an editor should change first:
- the split between units 3 and 7: 'things' and 'describing' overlap;
- `targetNewWords`, which is a guess at pacing and adds up to ~400 words,
short of the ~1 500 that docs/CONTENT.md wants for a complete A2;
- the Phase-0 sample unit `unit-1` in the database covers the same ground as
unit 1 here and should be retired or merged;
- `grammar` on each skill is an editor's note in English, not learner copy,
and several of the claims in it want a tutor's eye.
Learner-facing titles live in packages/i18n under `titleKey`; the `title`
field here is the same string kept next to the proposal so an editor can read
the file on its own. `spine.test.ts` asserts the two never drift apart.

title.en: Say hello and say who you are
title.nb: Hils og si hvem du er
Hils på noen og si ha det

skills.grammar: Greetings are learned whole. molo to one person, molweni to more than one — the -ni is the first plural a learner meets, before any rule is stated.

title.en: Hear the difference between c, x and q
title.nb: Hør forskjellen på c, x og q

skills.grammar: The three basic clicks in lesson one, as sounds before they are words: c dental, x lateral, q palatal. The aspirated and nasalised variants come later.

title.en: Say yes, no and thank you

skills.grammar: ewe and hayi as free answers; enkosi as the one word a visitor uses most.

title.en: Say your name and where you are from
title.nb: Si hva du heter og hvor du er fra

skills.grammar: First person: ndi- on the verb, igama lam for 'my name'. Introduced as patterns to reuse, not as a paradigm to learn.

title.en: Name the people in your family
title.nb: Sett navn på folkene i familien din

skills.grammar: Kinship terms are class 1a (umama, utata, usisi): a bare u- prefix and an oo- plural, which is why they come before class 1 proper.
Class 1: um- for people (umntu, umfazi, umfundi). The subject concord u- on the verb agrees with it.

title.en: Talk about more than one person
title.nb: Snakk om flere enn én person

skills.grammar: Class 2: aba- as the plural of class 1, with subject concord ba-. The first place a learner sees agreement change with number.

title.nb: Sett navn på tingene rundt deg

title.en: Name the things in a home
title.nb: Sett navn på tingene i et hjem

skills.grammar: Everyday objects spread across classes 3 to 9. The class is a fact on the word, learned with the word, never guessed from its shape.

title.nb: Sett navn på dyr og planter

skills.grammar: Class 9/10 carries most animals (inja, inkomo, intaka); class 3/4 carries trees. Two pairs, contrasted.
The singular/plural pairings 3-4, 5-6, 7-8, 9-10, taught as pairs of real words rather than as a table.

title.en: Name the parts of the body

skills.grammar: Body parts are the classic mixed-class set (isandla/izandla, unyawo/iinyawo, ilizwi/amazwi) and make the plural pairings concrete. They are also what unit 10 needs.

title.nb: Sett navn på mat og drikke

skills.grammar: Food nouns, including the loans a Cape Town menu actually uses. Mass nouns like amanzi live in class 6 with no singular.

title.en: Say what you want and what you like
title.nb: Si hva du vil ha og hva du liker

skills.grammar: Present tense with ndi-ya- and the verbs an order needs: funa, thanda, cela, nika, biza. The verbs belong here, with the situation, not in a grammar unit of their own.
One to ten. isiXhosa numerals agree with the noun they count, which is left as a pattern here and taken up properly in unit 8.

title.nb: Snakk om å lage mat og spise

skills.grammar: Kitchen verbs and the vessels they take. The Gothenburg corpus is unusually rich here, which is why this skill exists at all.
phi 'where', and the direction words: phambili, emva, ecaleni, phezulu, phantsi.

title.nb: Sett navn på steder i en by

skills.grammar: Buildings and places, most of them class 7 or 9 loans (isikolo, isibhedlele, ivenkile).
Transport nouns and the verbs of movement: hamba, ya, fika, buya, khwela.
The locative e-...-ini and its lexicalised forms (ekhaya, esikolweni, eGoli). TUTOR-VALIDATE: xh-morph does not generate locatives, so every form here comes from the lexicon or a corpus.

title.nb: Sett navn på dagene og månedene

skills.grammar: Days and months, and the week/month/year nouns around them.

title.en: Say what time of day it is
title.nb: Si hvilken tid på dagen det er

skills.grammar: Parts of the day (ekuseni, emini, ngokuhlwa, ebusuku) and the words for now, today, yesterday, tomorrow.
Past tense -ile and nd(a)-. TUTOR-VALIDATE: xh-morph generates no verb forms at all, so every past form shown here has to come from a corpus sentence or an editor.

title.nb: Snakk om det som skal skje

skills.grammar: Future with -za ku-. Same caveat as the past: no generator, so no generated forms.
Colour words are relatives, not adjectives, and take a relative concord that changes with the noun's class.

title.en: Say how big or small something is
title.nb: Si hvor stort eller lite noe er

skills.grammar: The true adjectives are a closed set of about a dozen stems (khulu, ncinci, de, ninzi, bini...) and take the adjective concord.
Character and feeling words, mostly relatives again (mnandi, nzima, lungileyo).

title.en: Join a describing word to a noun
title.nb: Sett et beskrivende ord til et substantiv

skills.grammar: The relative concord per class. This is the skill concord_fill exists for, and it stays empty until a tutor validates the classes.

title.en: Shop at a market and a shop
title.nb: Handle på marked og i butikk

skills.grammar: thenga, thengisa and the nouns of a market. The -is- causative pair is worth noticing here, not drilling.
imali, ixabiso, irandi, and the tens and hundreds.

title.en: Ask how much and how many
title.nb: Spør hvor mye og hvor mange

skills.grammar: ngaphi and the quantifiers (-nke, -ninzi, -mbalwa), which agree with the class of what is being counted.

title.nb: Si hva slags arbeid du gjør

skills.grammar: umsebenzi is class 1 for the worker and class 3 for the work — the clearest example in the course of why class is not decoration.
funda/fundisa/umfundi/utitshala as one family, which is how isiXhosa vocabulary is actually built.
The verbs of a day: vuka, hlamba, tya, sebenza, buya, lala, joined with the time words from unit 6.
Illness words plus the body parts from unit 3: 'my head is sore' is the pattern, and it needs the possessive concord.
nceda, cela, khusela and the words for trouble. The imperative is the one verb form a visitor genuinely needs in a hurry.

title.nb: Vær høflig og be om unnskyldning

skills.grammar: uxolo does duty as sorry, excuse me and please, which surprises every English speaker and is worth a culture card.
